title: In Search of Excellence
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explores why true excellence is rare and how leaders can spot it when selecting people for roles or teams. It argues that aptitude and experience are merely table stakes, and that what separates excellent performers is their appetite for feedback and willingness to absorb criticism despite the sting. The author suggests probing how candidates talk about improving even in hobbies, and recommends asking people to demonstrate skills directly rather than relying solely on interviews or resumes, since those who are excellent tend to welcome demonstration while average performers avoid it.
points: Aptitude and experience are only table stakes; excellence requires actively seeking and using feedback.
How someone talks about improving at a hobby can reveal their capacity for self-improvement.
Skills demonstrations reveal more than interviews, and reactions to being asked to demonstrate are themselves revealing.
Leaders often settle for above-average candidates because true excellence doesn't fit familiar stereotypes.
quotes: The foundation for the highest competence in any role or skill is aptitude, knowledge, experience, and the drive to learn.
To attain a competence and quality that is extraordinary, a professional must constantly seek feedback, absorb what is actionable, and then incorporate it into their daily execution.
In too many cases, candidates who might be excellent are overlooked because they say the wrong thing or don’t fit the stereotype a leader is looking for.
Those who are highly talented and reach for excellence love to showcase their skills. Those who are just above average or less despise this demonstration.
Surround yourself with excellent people, and pretty soon, learning and feedback spread like wildfire.
